paras: The reported lynching of William and Louis Neglin, spelled "Nagler" in wire reports, was a news story of August 1888 in which a dispatch from Holbrook, Arizona Territory, stated that "outlaws" had lynched the two ranchers in Pleasant Valley, in the Tonto Basin. Within two weeks Arizona papers reported that the story was "not correct": William Neglin appeared alive in Winslow, and Louis, at first missing, was later reported safe. The dispatch ran nationally, but the corrections appeared only in Arizona weeklies, and year-end lists of lynchings still counted the brothers.

The dispatch placed the killings in the Tonto Basin or Pleasant Valley feud, which, in the Los Angeles Herald's version, had "started one year ago in a scheme to drive out ranchmen and others holding interests detrimental to sheep owners." Earlier in August armed men had hanged James Stott, James Scott and Jeff Wilson near Phoenix Park, and the St. Johns Herald noted that Scott had gone to Pleasant Valley after a horse he had loaned to "Neglin Bros." The Apache Review described the Neglins as German-born stock men who had come from Colorado a year or two before.

The dispatch, dated August 18, said that William and Louis Nagler, "ranchers and stock men," had been lynched by outlaws in Pleasant Valley, without further detail. It added that W. H. McRaigy, an Aztec Land and Cattle Company employee, had reached Holbrook after being ordered off the ranch and fired at several times. The Apache Review later wrote that "McRaney" had been warned out by a match-box top marked "GO" in charcoal, left in his cabin window by regulators who wanted no outsider to witness their work.

William Neglin, interviewed in Winslow, said that he and Louie left their ranch at the upper end of Pleasant Valley about the 20th, and that some eight miles out Louie turned off to visit the ranch of a Frenchman. Louie never rejoined him, and William rode on to Winslow, where he learned of the reported lynching. His account placed both brothers alive two days after the date of the Holbrook dispatch.

On August 30 the St. Johns Herald reported that the lynching story "was not correct" and that nothing had been heard of Louis since the 20th. A third brother, Charles, of Durango, Colorado, had telegraphed Constable McKenney at Winslow, who, "not knowing anything to the contrary," confirmed the report; Charles came to Arizona and joined a search toward Payson.

The Arizona Silver Belt had reported on September 1 that Louie was "safe at his ranch in Pleasant Valley," and the Arizona Weekly Enterprise added that he had been seen in Phoenix on September 4, "sound and well." On September 12 the Prescott Journal-Miner concluded that the rumored hanging "proves to have been untrue." No report of an arrest or an inquiry into McRaigy's expulsion appears in the coverage.

The Holbrook item ran on August 19 and 20 in dailies from St. Paul, Omaha, Savannah and Washington, usually headed "Ranchers Lynched by Outlaws." A fuller version in the Los Angeles Herald and the Seattle Post-Intelligencer called the brothers "unoffensive" or "inoffensive citizens," and the Seattle paper headed it "SHEPHERD CROOKS." Weekly digests dated it "on the 18th," and December year-end lists entered it under August 17 as a hanging by "Outlaws in Pleasant Valley."

The Arizona Silver Belt's editorial "A Reign of Terror" treated the dispatch as "most probably" a sequel to the Stott, Scott and Wilson lynching and blamed a Governor and officers who did not enforce the laws. The Apache Review, under "Bloody Tonto Basin," held that "Lynch law cannot be countenanced." The Winslow News, headed "Not Lynched," called the lynchers "the mob of Tonto Basin neck stretchers" and the Neglins "peaceable and law abiding citizens." The corrections were brief local items, and the national papers that printed the lynching carried no retraction in the coverage found.

The Apache Review said "late advices confirm" the lynching, but the Winslow News based its denial on its editor's meeting with William in person, the more direct evidence. The wire spelled the surname "Nagler" and the Silver Belt "Nogler," while local papers that knew the family wrote "Neglin."

accounts.label: Holbrook wire
accounts.gist: Outlaws in Pleasant Valley lynched William and Louis Nagler, inoffensive ranchers, as part of the sheep and cattle feud; McRaigy was ordered off and shot at.

accounts.label: Arizona Silver Belt editorial
accounts.gist: Took the dispatch as true and as probably a sequel to the Stott, Scott and Wilson lynching, blaming lax enforcement of the law.

accounts.label: William Neglin (via Winslow News)
accounts.gist: He and Louie left their ranch about the 20th; Louie turned off to visit a Frenchman and did not rejoin him; William learned of the reported lynching on reaching Winslow.

accounts.label: Apache Review
accounts.gist: Said 'late advices confirm' that the Neglin brothers were lynched about the time of the Stott lynching, and that a sworn band of eighty-six regulators was at work.

accounts.label: Arizona corrections
accounts.gist: The report was 'not correct' and the rumored hanging 'untrue'; Louis was safe at his ranch or seen in Phoenix.

framing.detail: National dailies ran the Holbrook item as 'Ranchers Lynched by Outlaws', with the Seattle Post-Intelligencer heading it 'SHEPHERD CROOKS' and calling the Naglers 'inoffensive' (A3).
The Arizona Silver Belt's 'A Reign of Terror' blamed 'outlaws' and a Governor and officers who did not enforce the laws.
The Apache Review said 'Lynch law cannot be countenanced' but also reported citizens' claim that thieves had exhausted their patience.
The Winslow News, headed 'Not Lynched', called the lynchers 'the mob of Tonto Basin neck stretchers' and the Neglins 'peaceable and law abiding'.
The St. Johns Herald and Journal-Miner printed brief corrections.
